title: Reading 9: Functions of innovation systems: a new approach for analysing technological change

chapters.title: The paper in brief
paragraphs: The authors start from a claim about why some technologies spread and others do not. Innovation systems, they argue, are an important determinant of technological change, and the emergence of a new system co-evolves with the technology itself. Their problem is that the usual way of analysing such systems does not capture this. Most studies compare structures, so they describe a system as it stands rather than how it changes, and they explain performance through institutions rather than through what entrepreneurs do (page 414).

Their answer is to study what happens inside a system. They call the relevant activities functions of innovation systems, and they propose seven of them: entrepreneurial activities, knowledge development, knowledge diffusion through networks, guidance of the search, market formation, resource mobilization, and the creation of legitimacy (pages 421-425). The unit of analysis is a technology specific innovation system, which takes a technology rather than a region or a sector as its starting point (page 416).

The paper is conceptual. Its examples come from Sustainable Technology Development: solar cells, hydrogen, biofuels in Germany and the Netherlands, and biomass gasification. The seven functions themselves draw on empirical studies at Utrecht University (page 421). The method they propose is process analysis, or history event analysis. Events are collected from newspapers and professional journals, allocated to the seven functions, rated as positive or negative, and plotted over time (pages 427-428).

The findings are about how the functions behave together. The authors argue that fulfilling one function quite likely affects the others, and they expect a non-linear model with many interactions (pages 425-426). Following Jacobsson and Johnson, they describe virtuous cycles that build momentum. Seven functions allow many interactions, but their empirical work shows that developments often start from a few functions that pull the others. Figure 2 shows three such patterns, which they call motors of change (page 426). They also allow for vicious cycles, and give biomass gasification as the example (page 427). First studies of biomass digestion, biomass gasification and biofuels in the Netherlands, they report, found that the functions fit the empirical data well (page 428).

The contribution the authors claim is a framework that makes system dynamics visible and gives policy a set of targets. They say it makes comparison between systems with different institutional set-ups easier, allows a more systematic mapping of the determinants of innovation, and can deliver policy targets and instruments (page 420). They are careful about the word function. They reject the positivist and organic assumptions of functionalism, prefer Merton's middle-range propositions, and keep the term for its heuristic value only (page 429).

The paper is a core reading for Lecture 6, Technological innovation systems, where it supplies the seven functions the lecture introduces before its Norwegian carbon capture case. That case is assessed with a related but longer list of functions, so the two lists are not identical. For the December 2024 exam, Question 3 asked how technologies in innovation systems can promote or inhibit sustainable transformation. The lecture answers that question with the functions. The paper's own advice fits: assess how well each function is fulfilled, then stimulate the weak ones or remove blocking mechanisms (page 430). Here is an example of our own, not from the paper: a new technology can have excellent laboratories behind it and still fail because no one has built a market for it.

checks.q: What method do the authors propose for mapping the functions?
checks.a: Process analysis, or history event analysis: events are collected from newspapers and professional journals, allocated to the seven functions, rated positive or negative, and plotted over time.

checks.q: What are the seven functions of innovation systems?
checks.a: Entrepreneurial activities, knowledge development, knowledge diffusion through networks, guidance of the search, market formation, resource mobilization, and the creation of legitimacy.

chapters.title: Why a structural view of innovation systems was not enough
paragraphs: The abstract and the first lines of the introduction set up the argument. The authors say innovation systems are an important determinant of technological change, and that the emergence of a new system and changes in existing ones co-evolve with that change. Traditional analysis, which focuses on the structure of innovation systems, has proved insufficient. They therefore propose a framework built on processes they call functions of innovation systems, plus a method of process analysis or history event analysis to map them. The examples come from Sustainable Technology Development.

The introduction defines its terms. Technological change here means technology developing in interaction with the system in which it is embedded, and an innovation is a successful combination of hardware, software and orgware, where orgware is the components of the innovation system. The authors then name two shortcomings of the innovation system framework. Most analyses are quasi-static, comparing structures rather than dynamics. And the framework's explanatory power lies in institutions at the macro level, not in the actions of the entrepreneur at the micro level.

The authors state the central idea: analysis should map the activities that result in technological change, and these are called functions. Section 2 sets out the innovation system approach, in which innovation is both an individual and a collective act. An innovation system is defined as the institutions and economic structures that affect the rate and direction of technological change. Freeman calls it a network of institutions whose activities and interactions bring in, change and spread new technologies. The systemic character of change, the authors add, explains why change is slow and why systems lock in.

The authors adopt the concept of a technological system, where the starting point is a technology rather than a region or a sector. They give Carlsson and Stankiewicz's definition, a network of agents that interact under an institutional infrastructure and generate, diffuse and use a technology. Lundvall, they add, also treats technological systems as a version of innovation systems, and notes that most innovation policy supports existing systems rather than new ones. Hughes's Large Technological Systems include physical artifacts; the authors exclude them and call their object a Technology Specific Innovation System.

checks.q: What two shortcomings of the innovation system framework do the authors identify?
checks.a: That most analyses are quasi-static and compare structures rather than dynamics, and that the framework's explanatory power lies in institutions at the macro level rather than in the actions of the entrepreneur at the micro level.

checks.q: How does a technology specific innovation system differ from Hughes's Large Technological Systems?
checks.a: The Large Technological Systems include physical artifacts, while the technology specific system takes a technology and its agents as the starting point and leaves those artifacts out.

chapters.title: From mapping structure to mapping functions
paragraphs: Figure 1 shows the boundary relations: one technology specific innovation system overlapping four national systems and three sectoral ones, which are themselves inside national systems. The authors then argue that dynamics are hard to map at national level, because the number of actors, networks and institutions is extreme. Studies of national systems therefore focus on current structure, using indicators such as R&D, patents, the quality of education, university-industry collaboration and venture capital. In a technology specific system the number of actors is much smaller, so a dynamic analysis becomes possible.

The authors give an example of why dynamics matter. Germany and the Netherlands both support renewable energy, but Germany diffuses it faster. A structural comparison would show that German producers receive higher prices and longer contracts. A dynamic analysis would add how those regulations came about: the lobby, the opposition, external events, and the co-evolution of rules and learning. Because many activities take place in a system, only relevant ones should be mapped, meaning those that influence the system's goal of developing, applying and diffusing new technological knowledge.

The authors review earlier lists of functions. Galli and Teubal separate hard functions, which need organizations performing R&D, from soft ones such as diffusion, policy making and standard setting. Liu and White name five activities: research, implementation, end-use, linkage and education. Johnson identifies eight system functions, from supplying incentives and resources to guiding the search, creating markets and providing legitimacy. The authors note that Johnson's set is written in an active sense, so that it is close to a set of policy recommendations.

The authors trace how Johnson's eight functions were reduced to five in later empirical work: creating new knowledge, guiding the search, supplying resources, creating positive external economies, and forming markets. They give three reasons for adopting a functions approach. It makes comparison between systems with different institutional set-ups easier. It gives a more systematic way of mapping the determinants of innovation. And it can deliver policy targets and instruments. The page ends with a list from Smits and Kuhlmann, two of this paper's own authors, of functions that policy instruments should support.

checks.q: Why is a technology specific innovation system easier to analyse dynamically than a national one?
checks.a: Because it contains far fewer actors, networks and relevant institutions, which reduces complexity and makes a dynamic analysis possible at that level of aggregation.

checks.q: What five activities do Liu and White focus on?
checks.a: Research, implementation, end-use, linkage and education.

chapters.title: Seven functions for analysing an innovation system
paragraphs: The page finishes the policy argument. Smits and Kuhlmann say innovation processes need instruments that support functions such as providing platforms for learning and an infrastructure for strategic intelligence. The authors add that system-level instruments exist, such as standards and foresight programmes, but that evaluations in OECD countries find policy portfolios still dominated by financial support for R&D in individual firms. Section 5 then proposes the authors' own seven functions and describes the first: entrepreneurial activities, in which entrepreneurs turn the potential of new knowledge, networks and markets into action.

Entrepreneurs' risky experiments cope with uncertainty and teach actors about the technology. Active entrepreneurs are a first sign of system performance; when they lag, the cause may lie in the other six functions. Van de Ven asks which functions a firm performs itself, and with which organizations it links or competes. Dutch biofuel firms lobbied together for a tax exemption while competing for R&D money. Suurs and Hekkert found diversifying incumbents more active in fulfilling system functions than start-ups. Function 2, knowledge development, covers learning by searching and by doing, mapped through R&D projects, patents and R&D investment.

Function 3 is knowledge diffusion through networks, which the authors call a precondition for learning by interacting and, in user-producer networks, for learning by using. Function 4 is guidance of the search. Because resources are limited, choices must be made among technological options, and this selection can be made by industry, government or the market. The authors give examples: a Dutch goal of 10% renewable energy in 2020, and Californian rules obliging car makers to sell zero emission vehicles by 2003. Frenken and colleagues showed that the Californian goal raised R&D on low emission vehicles.

The page continues guidance of the search with hydrogen: its promise as a clean fuel raises expectations that encourage research funding, and the words policy makers use signal those expectations. Function 5 is market formation. New technologies struggle against embedded ones, so they need protected space, such as temporary niche markets, or a temporary advantage through favourable taxes or minimum consumption quotas. In Germany, a tax exemption made biofuels cost the same as fossil fuels, and they reached many gas stations. In the Netherlands, the lack of a structural exemption blocked such initiatives.

Function 6 is resource mobilization, meaning financial and human capital. The authors note that this function is hard to measure over time, so the best method is to ask core actors in interviews whether access to resources is a problem. Function 7 is the creation of legitimacy, or countering resistance to change. Parties with vested interests may oppose a new technology, and advocacy coalitions can put it on the agenda, lobby for resources and favourable tax rules, and so build legitimacy. The authors illustrate this with the German biofuels lobby, which grew from farmers' subsidies into the UFOP.

checks.q: What is the authors' first function, and what does it cover?
checks.a: Entrepreneurial activities: entrepreneurs turn the potential of new knowledge, networks and markets into concrete actions, and they can be new entrants or incumbent firms diversifying their business.

checks.q: Why is resource mobilization hard to analyse over time, and how do the authors suggest mapping it?
checks.a: Because it is difficult to capture with specific indicators, so the best method is to detect through interviews whether core actors perceive access to sufficient resources as problematic.

chapters.title: Motors of change, process analysis and the functionalist worry
paragraphs: Functions influence one another, the authors argue, so a non-linear model with many interactions is to be expected. Following Jacobsson and Johnson, they say fulfilment can produce virtuous cycles that build momentum for creative destruction. Seven functions allow many interactions, but the authors' empirical work shows developments often start from a few functions that pull the others. Figure 2 shows three such patterns, called motors of change. In sustainable technologies, a common trigger is guidance of the search: government goals bring resources, then knowledge and rising expectations. Another is entrepreneurs lobbying for resources or for market formation.

Vicious cycles are also possible: in Dutch biomass gasification, high expectations met poor results from demonstration projects, disappointment spread, and the system took years to recover. System change, the authors argue, happens only when functions reach certain thresholds, so the order of events matters, and the dominant variance approach, which ignores that order, is inadequate. The process approach, or sequence analysis, explains outcomes by the sequence of events and tells a story line. Its unit is the event. Van de Ven's Minnesota studies mapped events around single projects; the authors collect system-level events from newspaper archives and professional journals.

These events, such as workshops, new R&D projects, expectations in the press and announced resources, are allocated to the seven functions. This also tests the list: many events that fit no function would show it is incomplete. First studies of biomass digestion, biomass gasification and biofuels in the Netherlands found that the functions fit the data well. Each event is rated positive or negative, and seven plots over time support a storyline, from which cross-case analysis seeks general patterns. Section 8 then names functionalism's two features: an objective social world studied like nature, and society modelled on an organism.

The authors share the criticisms of both features. Against positivism, they stress that social reality is contingent and reflexive, citing their focus on entrepreneurs. In the organic view, agents serve the survival of the whole, like organs in a body, and Parsons even saw the world as a system of societies. The authors prefer Merton's middle-range propositions to grand theory, and keep the word function for its heuristic value, not its positivistic one. Section 9 begins the conclusions: the innovation system concept is useful but too static and too little concerned with the micro level.

checks.q: What does the authors' term motors of change refer to?
checks.a: Three initial patterns of interaction, shown in Figure 2, in which a limited number of functions pull the others and set a virtuous cycle going.

checks.q: Why do the authors prefer the process approach to the variance approach?
checks.a: Because the variance approach ignores the order of events, while system change depends on thresholds and sequence, and the process approach explains outcomes as the result of that order.

chapters.title: Conclusions and the reference list
paragraphs: The conclusions close the argument: mapping functions over time gives insight into dynamics, and process analysis suits this because it treats change as a sequence of events. The authors say the insight is likely to be highly relevant for policy. A first step is to understand how the relevant system currently functions, and the next is to deploy systemic instruments that stimulate weak functions or remove blocking mechanisms. They call for further theoretical and empirical work. The page then carries the acknowledgements and the start of the reference list.
These pages are the reference list.

checks.q: What do the authors say policy should do with the functions?
checks.a: Use insight into how the relevant system currently functions, then deploy systemic instruments that stimulate weak functions or remove blocking mechanisms.
